item.title: Aaron Ford flips Nevada governorship, becoming state’s first Black governor

media:content.media:title: Nevada Gov.-elect Aaron Ford greets supporters after speaking at an election night event on Nov. 4, 2026, in Las Vegas.

item.dc:creator: By Jalen Beckford
item.content:encoded:
Democrat Aaron Ford won Nevada’s gubernatorial race, ousting Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the first Black person elected to lead the battleground state.

Ford’s victory gives Democrats a key pickup and elevates the two-term attorney general, who made his working-class upbringing and ties to organized labor central to his campaign. He joins a growing list of Black governors-elect, following earlier victories by Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in Florida.

Ford, a native of Dallas, campaigned on building more affordable housing, expanding union apprenticeship programs and repealing the state’s right-to-work law, with backing from the powerful Culinary Union.

His win returns the governor’s office to Democratic control four years after Lombardo defeated Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak. Ford overcame the incumbent’s substantial financial advantage in a race that tested Democrats’ efforts to win over working-class voters.

The result is a turnaround for Democrats in a state Donald Trump carried by 3 percentage points in 2024, and it gives the party an opening to rebuild support in a major battleground state ahead of 2028.

item.title: Arizona, Nebraska voters approve transgender athlete bans

media:content.media:title: A person holds a sign advocating for a ban on transgender women and girls in women's and girls' sports outside the Supreme Court on June 29, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Bianca Quilantan
item.content:encoded:
The conservative movement to bar transgender athletes from women’s sports showed its message could resonate beyond Republican strongholds.

Voters in Arizona — a state with a Democratic governor and senators — approved a ballot initiative further restricting transgender students from participating on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

The measure expands the state’s existing ban on trans athletes participating on women’s school sports teams, adds restrictions on locker-room use and defines a person’s sex based on their original birth certificate.

Similar measures in Colorado and Washington state are leading in early results, though votes are still being counted. In Nebraska, voters also added a ban to their state constitution.

The issue has found a champion in President Donald Trump, who has pushed a suite of anti-trans federal policies since returning to the White House.

But conservatives had made little progress outside the red states that swiftly passed bans in recent years. The measures on the ballot this year marked the first time voters had the chance to weigh in on the issue. The measures’ success could fuel similar campaigns to bypass resistant legislatures in more states.

item.title: Trump’s two new tormenters: Courts and Congress
item.description: The president enters his final chapter in public office in an unfamiliar position.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) are seen during a watch party at the AC Hotel Capitol Hill on Election Day in Washington, on Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kyle Cheney
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump awakens Wednesday boxed in. Already in the pincer grip of federal courts that have slowed his agenda, he now faces a historically powerful incoming Democratic majority in Congress, eager to turn their gavels and subpoena power on their longtime tormentor.

And he’ll face them down while a new crop of Republicans seeks to eclipse him as the leader of their party.

This is how the last chapter of the Trump era in Washington begins.

For Trump, it’s an unfamiliar position. He has spent a decade seeking to project invincibility and has spent the first two years of his second term asserting unprecedented executive power with little pushback from a Republican-controlled Congress. He sought to salvage that reputation with a social media post as Republican losses piled up.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote Tuesday night.

Not exactly a salve for a party in crisis.

Democrats also face a choice: how much of their investigative muscle and political capital are they willing to spend investigating a weakened Trump. The party continues to see Trump as a useful, unifying foil. Some of their incoming members have flirted with seeking to impeach him a third time, though Democratic leaders have not committed to that course.

If there was any doubt about the House’s intent, however, Rep. Robert Garcia — expected to lead the House Oversight Committee — erased it quickly.

“LAWYER UP,” Garcia posted on X Tuesday night, just as news outlets began calling the House for Democrats. Garcia and other House allies have projected a muscular investigative agenda aimed at what they have described as Trump’s corruption and alleged self-enrichment, his abuses of executive power, his misuse of pardons for the politically and financially connected and his decision to empower ICE to lead a mass deportation campaign.

Trump has never willingly ceded the spotlight — and has never needed to. Before Tuesday, he was at his weakest point in 2021, shortly after a mob of his supporters attacked the Capitol and Republican leaders seemed poised to abandon him. But because he remained politically viable, those leaders quickly returned to the fold, helping engineer his return to power and beat back impeachment and a fusillade of criminal charges.

Now, though, there is no political future for Trump, who is in his final two years of elected office. And it was in that context that he signaled a rare conciliatory approach Tuesday.

“We’re going to work with the Democrats to make sure things go well for our country,” he said in an interview with POLITICO’s Dasha Burns on POLITICO Elections Live. “I don’t want to sit here for two years just vetoing everything.”

item.title: Capitol agenda: GOP suffers historic rebuke
item.description: Democrats swept both chambers of Congress as Republicans faced generational-level losses across the country.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks alongside Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and other congressional Democrats during a press event outside the U.S. Capitol on May 21, 2026. (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images)

item.dc:creator: By Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
A new age of Democratic power is coming to Washington.

The party Tuesday swept both chambers of Congress as Republicans faced generational-level losses across the country. As of publication time, Democrats have won at least 54 Senate seats and have flipped about 20 House seats, with many competitive races still uncalled. Voters pummeled the GOP out of power and effectively cemented President Donald Trump’s lame-duck era.

Ahead of the election, most senior House Democrats dared not imagine more than a 10-seat majority. Now it’s looking like 250 seats or more are not out of the question — all but assuring Hakeem Jeffries will cruise to the speakership.

In the Senate, Democrats won Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, sent a Texan to the chamber after a more than 30-year absence, broke a nearly 30-year losing streak in South Carolina and elected the first Iowan in more than a decade.

They could even be on the cusp of a Mississippi Senate seat for the first time in roughly four decades. Scott Colom has a less than 50-vote lead on Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as we write. The Alaska race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola also remains in tossup territory.

Longtime GOP incumbents like Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Missouri Rep. Ann Wagner are out of jobs. NRCC Chair Richard Hudson is hanging by a thread, as is House Rules Chair Rep. Virginia Foxx — both caught in a ticketwide GOP collapse in North Carolina.

Also decimated: the corps of Republican moderates on Capitol Hill, including Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Jen Kiggans of Virginia.

The massive gains in both chambers, unthinkable even a few months ago, will have an instant impact. Republicans’ hopes to check off a list of priority legislation in the lame-duck session are in jeopardy, and they will quickly have to confront questions about their leadership.

Trump’s once ironclad grip over Washington is also in question, as he can no longer flex his influence over a Republican-led Congress willing to bend to his whims and waive away allegations of his administration’s corruption. Some in his party are also beginning to contemplate their future after he leaves the White House.

“Voters all across America have spoken, and this is a wake-up call for all conservatives,” said South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman, arguing the GOP needed to “start governing on the core principles they campaigned on.”

What else we’re watching: 

— GOP LEADERSHIP HAZY: Speaker Mike Johnson’s political future is now up in the air with the House majority lost under his watch. Several Republicans prior to the election doubted he would jump into the race to become minority leader. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan could jump into the running to become the top House Republican as soon as Wednesday, ahead of a Friday deadline to announce their candidacy. The GOP conference will vote next week. Trump, pressed on whether he backs Johnson to return as minority leader, did not answer directly. “I think he’s done a very good job,” Trump told POLITICO Tuesday night. “I mean, they’re going to have to make that decision. He’s going to have to make that decision. But he’s a good person and a good man.” Many House Republicans were already speculating early this morning if the entire leadership team could get swept up in the GOP loss.

— ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS READY PROBES — Democrats’ sweep of Congress sets the stage for an unrelenting oversight platform next year. Democrats plan to use their new subpoena power and agenda-setting authority to target possible corruption among members of Trump’s family, Elon Musk’s leadership of the Department of Government Efficiency and the Department of Homeland Security’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics, according to interviews with more than a dozen lawmakers, aides and attorneys. “LAWYER UP,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on House Oversight, posted on social media Tuesday as the party’s House majority was coming into focus.

Dasha Burns, Mia McCarthy and Chris Marquette contributed to this report.

item.dc:creator: By Aaron Pellish
item.content:encoded:
Democrats’ massive blue wave could get even bigger, as a handful of key races remain uncalled.

Senate
Alaska: Votes in the battleground Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are still being counted.

Mississippi: Just 43 votes separate Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The state does not allow recounts, even by request of either candidate, so the final tally will be determinative in that state.

HouseAnd a handful of House Republicans are awaiting calls in their races, including the following notable names:

  • Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), the person responsible for getting House Republicans elected. The NRCC chair is locked in a tight battle against Democrat Richard Ojeda.
  • Colorado GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert, who's trying to fend off Democrat Eileen Laubacher.
  • Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.), who's neck and neck with Democrat Leela Gray.

item.title: Democrats are about to run the show on Capitol Hill. What will they do with their power?
item.description: The party will be under pressure to legislate alongside its aggressive oversight ambitions.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is joined on stage by Reps. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) after delivering remarks at a watch party at the AC Hotel Capitol Hill on Election Day in Washington, on Nov. 3, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Kelsey Brugger
item.content:encoded:
Democrats will control Congress next year. And once they’re done celebrating their decisive midterm victory, they’ll have to confront their next challenge: leveraging their power to legislate with President Donald Trump still in the White House the next two years.

While much of Democrats’ time will be spent wielding their new subpoena power to haul in Trump’s top officials and allies, they have no shortage of ideas for policies they also want to pursue — on everything from technology and artificial intelligence to health care and taxes.

Many of the proposals Democrats put forward will inevitably be messaging bills that try to shape public opinion ahead of the presidential contest in 2028 — and lay the groundwork for a legislative agenda they can jump on if they win a governing trifecta that year.

“We'll aggressively prepare to get off to a fast start on January 3rd in the new Congress,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, on track to become speaker, said in an October press call.

The party will honor its commitments, he continued, to “relentlessly focus on the affordability crisis” and “drive down the high cost of living, because life is way too expensive in the United States of America.”

Democrats will ultimately be under enormous pressure to show they can actually get things done, including within their own caucus, where progressive members will be fighting for influence against moderates. Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer — set to be the Senate majority leader in the new Congress — will have to carefully navigate those divisions to secure unity, even on party-line bills.

Progressives are going to push to advance policies like a wealth tax, “Medicare for All” and strict regulation of AI that could involve a ban on developing “superintelligence.”

“Next year, Democrats must pass bills powerful enough to actually tackle the cost of living crisis and root out rampant corruption. We cannot be the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges,” Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas said in a statement in the days leading up to the midterms.

Casar was responding directly to the likely incoming No. 2 Senate Democrat, Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who suggested on CNN that Democrats should wait until 2028 to “make more bold policy changes.”

Moderates may be looking to rework bipartisan bills that have languished during the Republican governing trifecta while pushing back against proposals they view as too extreme.

The debate over regulating AI will be one where warring Democratic factions could come to blows over how to rein in a potentially dangerous technology without stifling innovation and ceding ground to China. Progressives, led by Casar and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, are pushing to pause advanced AI development and ban superintelligence, which more centrist lawmakers say is untenable.

“The [AI] discussion so far is … pretty populist, pretty devoid of fact, and I think we have to be more realistic about it,” Rep. Scott Peters of California, a moderate Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said in a recent interview.

The easiest way for Democrats to achieve legislative victories will be by jamming Republicans on must-pass bills, such as for government funding, a debt ceiling increase and the annual defense policy measure. Otherwise, Democrats could find bipartisan potential around issues like cryptocurrency if lawmakers are unable to finalize an industry overhaul during the post-midterm “lame-duck” session. The same goes for passing a farm bill and legislation to reauthorize surface transportation programs.

Democrats could also try to entice GOP privacy hawks, like Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, with legislation to rein in the proliferation of Flock cameras, which automatically capture moving vehicles and can share the data with law enforcement.

Some Democrats will also push to restore some clean energy subsidies after Republicans slashed several renewable tax credit programs as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025. Both Jeffries and Schumer have said they would introduce legislation to restore the phased-out wind and solar credits, but they could run into opposition from some industry players who want to disprove arguments from Republicans that renewables can’t compete without help.

Health care is another area where Democrats could find themselves divided. The party will need to decide whether to preserve the 2010 Affordable Care Act’s formula of expanding the health insurance safety net bit by bit — or propose blowing up the system through “Medicare For All.”

Progressive Reps. Debbie Dingell of Michigan and Linda Sánchez of California — senior members of Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, respectively — are expected to be among those pushing the latter option following an election cycle centered on Americans struggling to pay bills. If successful, the effort would plant a flag going into 2028 and signal that Democrats no longer fear backlash from voters who prefer their private plans.

Democrats could come together in seeking to undo the $1 trillion in cuts to Medicaid that Republicans enacted in last year’s megalaw, restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that Republicans allowed to expire at the end of 2025 and expand the Medicare drug price negotiation program they created during their last governing trifecta in in the 2022.

“We can have reasonable prices for these drugs, and guess what? These pharmaceutical companies, they'll be just fine,” Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), who was influential during the drug price negotiations at that time, said in an interview in September.

In any event, Democrats will need to move quickly to implement an affordability agenda in line with their campaign promises to lower the cost of living. Proposals include legislation to prohibit grocery store price gouging, expand the child tax credit and reverse Republican cuts to federal nutrition programs.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is expected to become the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has also consistently pushed follow-up legislation to the bipartisan housing package that became law in July. She could team up on that effort with Rep. Maxine Waters of California — though her House Financial Services gavel is up in the air as the 88-year-old fends off possible challenges from Illinois Democratic Reps. Sean Casten, 54, and Bill Foster, 71.

More broadly, though, some Democrats have been eager to downplay divisions in their party.

“At the end of the day, the things we don’t agree with, we'll figure out,” said one House Democratic aide granted anonymity to speak candidly. “I don’t think folks will want to come out of the gate with a circular firing squad.”

Simon J. Levien, Katherine Hapgood, Brian Faler, Gabby Miller, Owen Dahlkamp, Jasper Goodman, Ari Hawkins, Nico Portuondo, Connor O’Brien, Mackenzie Wilkes, Robert King, Alice Miranda Ollstein, and Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

item.title: Democrats are ready to run Congress — and investigate all things Trump
item.description: The party will face a challenge in messaging how an aggressive oversight agenda will make life better for Americans.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) discusses what he called the "DOGE DEMOLITION PLAN" while Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) looks on during the first hearing of the House Oversight and Accountability Subcommittee on Delivering on Government Efficiency hearing on Capitol Hill Feb. 12, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Chris Marquette
item.content:encoded:
Democrats have taken back the House and Senate, setting the stage for an unrelenting oversight platform in the next Congress that will zero in on both the Trump administration and the special interests that Republicans were reluctant to scrutinize over the last two years.

According to interviews with more than a dozen lawmakers, aides and attorneys, Democrats plan to use their new subpoena power and agenda-setting authority to target possible corruption among members of President Donald Trump’s family, Elon Musk’s leadership of the Department of Government Efficiency and the Department of Homeland Security’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics.

They could demand testimony from the chief executives of Big Tech on social media addiction, the dangers of artificial intelligence and the negative impacts data centers are having on local communities. They could haul in the heads of leading oil companies to answer for allegations the industry waged a decadeslong climate misinformation campaign to continue reaping massive profits.

And these are just a few items on the to-do list.

“I’d expect some pretty epic battles between the administration and Congress, as well as private sector targets that are prepared to fight back against Congress,” said Aaron Cutler, a partner at Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and former aide to former House Majority Leader Eric Cantor.

Many major Washington law firms, expecting a favorable night for Democrats, have already started hiring experienced lawyers to help their clients navigate new congressional scrutiny, Cutler added.

“LAWYER UP,” Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, posted on social media Tuesday as the party’s House majority was coming into focus.

The risk, however, is that Democrats’ vast investigative ambitions backfire, sucking up oxygen that might otherwise be spent trying to legislate. Though Trump is unlikely to sign many, if any, bills Democrats send to his desk that aren’t considered “must-pass,” Democrats will still be under pressure to show they can do something, even if it’s just laying the groundwork for a legislative agenda the party can enact if they also retake the White House in 2028.

“I think we would put the priority on things that have had an impact on cost of living for the American people — so any kind of corruption with the administration that has raised costs,” said Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who, as a member of the House, led impeachment proceedings against the president in the first Trump administration.

Schiff suggested one such potential line of inquiry could be into Amazon.

“If federal contracting decisions are made not because a vendor has the best product or is offering it for the best price, but because, in the case of Amazon, it was willing to pay $40 million for a crappy movie about Melania [Trump], is that resulting in Amazon getting an advantage in cloud computing contracts or other defense contracts — that's the kind of thing that costs taxpayers money, costs consumers more money, and there have been so many business payoffs of one sort or another,” said Schiff, referring to the first lady.

Over in the House, Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey, the top Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, wants to look into surveillance pricing, in which AI tools track a customer's online habits to determine how much they should be paying for basic goods like groceries — and potentially driving up costs for everyone in the process. It’s an issue that energizes progressives, like Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas, as well as Republicans: Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri held a hearing on the issue in August.

Democrats are likewise expected to build on their oversight of data centers, including operators’ commitments to cover the full energy costs associated with their infrastructure, according to several senior committee Democrats and Democratic congressional aides.

They say they will also try to expose ways in which the administration’s actions could be contributing to high energy prices and more pollution, from the Iran war to the cancellation and slow-walking of renewable energy projects. Inquiries into prescription drug pricing could also lead to policy recommendations aimed at lowering health care costs.

But Democrats also could be heading towards a clash with some members intent on pursuing a more partisan, take-no-prisoners approach toward their oversight duties.

For instance, Garcia and Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committees, have made clear they consider the Jeffrey Epstein investigation unfinished business. Raskin, a week before the midterms, released a staff report detailing sexual assault allegations against Trump by five separate women in a possible preview of the lines of inquiry Democrats could pursue.

The possibility that Democrats could undertake politically divisive impeachment proceedings against any number of Cabinet officials also looms large. Some Democrats are eager to oust the president himself, with Raskin saying over the summer he would not rule that out — even though the party is certain to remain well short of the two-thirds needed to convict in the Senate.

“I want to go straight to the top: Donald Trump,” Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pa.), a member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in an interview regarding impeachment. “And then everybody who was complicit in allowing him to do what he's done, or working in concert with him on illegal things.”

One person in Trump’s orbit likely to absorb much of Democrats’ scrutiny is Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is already the subject of a House impeachment effort.

Hegseth and the Defense Department could face even more scrutiny next year if Rep. Adam Smith, the Washington Democrat in line to be the next chair of the House Armed Services Committee, decides to revive a subcommittee dedicated solely to Pentagon oversight issues.

Smith will need to balance a need to reach bipartisan compromise on an annual defense policy package with the whole list of Pentagon controversies his members want to pursue. That includes a full accounting of the cost and impact of the Iran war, politicization of the military and Hegseth’s own performance.

“To be candid, Donald Trump should have already fired this guy,” Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), a member of the Armed Services Committee, said in an interview. “I think this Iran war has been disastrous. It's a major part of contributing to the cost of living emergency. American people are mad about it.”

On the House Ways and Means Committee, Democrats want to put forward new proposals to expand the popular child tax credit and beef up breaks for child-care expenses, and potentially work with Republicans on tax issues relating to retirees. The Senate Finance Committee could take up an idea floated over the summer by the likely incoming Senate Democratic Leader, Chuck Schumer, to quadruple a tax on stock buybacks by corporations.

But Democratic taxwriters are just as likely to spend next year scrutinizing the controversial decision to excuse Trump from IRS audits as part of a broader settlement between the president and the Justice Department, as well as the tax agency’s collaboration with Homeland Security to crack down on illegal immigration. They’ve also signaled plans to look into the tech industry’s use of corporate tax breaks, including whether Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s should be allowed to claim a research subsidy in conjunction with his company’s data center construction.

Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), who are expected to return as chairs of House Ways and Means and Senate Finance, could face renewed calls to seize Trump’s still-hidden tax returns — a demand both men contended with during the first Trump administration.

The Senate’s primary oversight panel, the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, could center on DHS’s execution of the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.

Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.), who is in line to chair Homeland Security next year, has spent the past year building a team to help her use her position to “investigate and hold President Trump and his Administration accountable for its widespread corruption and wrongdoing,” said a person granted anonymity to describe her private planning. Members of that team have experience working in the White House, DHS and the Department of Health and Human Services.

Hassan’s staff, the person said, will deploy resources to focus on “egregious” wrongdoing where there is “clear disapproval from the majority of Americans.”

Ari Hawkins, Andres Picon, Alfred Ng, Brian Faler, Connor O’Brien, Gabby Miller and Owen Dahlkamp contributed to this report.

item.title: What Hakeem Jeffries’ Albany years reveal about how he’d lead the House
item.description: The moderate Democrat developed a signature style in the New York capital that will be put to the test next year if his party wins the House.

media:content.media:title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 30, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Joe Anuta, Nick Reisman and Bill Mahoney
item.dc:contributor: By Joe Anuta, Nick Reisman and Bill Mahoney
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — On the road to becoming House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries toiled for years under top-heavy leadership. He bore witness to corruption in the highest ranks of government. And, as he rose in stature, he established himself as a persuasive orator, hyper-engaged colleague and prolific fundraiser.

And that was before he got to Congress.

As the 56-year-old legislator seeks to become the first Black speaker of the House, clues to how he engineered such a rapid rise — and how he’ll govern if Democrats win the House — can be traced back to the rough-and-tumble world of statehouse politics in New York, where he served as an assemblymember representing parts of Brooklyn from 2007 through 2012.

While in Albany, Jeffries hardly mastered the levers of power. He wasn’t around long enough to earn a committee chair position. He wasn’t senior enough to carry the conference’s marquee legislation. And he passed only a fraction of the 242 bills he sponsored.

Yet he carved out a legislative record establishing himself as a credible voice on criminal justice issues. And the lessons offered by Albany at the time — with half of its Legislature beset by factionalism and a hard-charging executive damaged by scandal — offered a valuable preview of what he could face in Washington.

Jeffries could inherit an unwieldy House. He could face a Senate with razor-thin margins. And he already has plans to launch probes into President Donald Trump and many of his aides.

But the leadership style he began developing in Albany is in many ways an odd fit with the current political moment.

In an age where voters are gravitating toward partisan pugilists, Albany colleagues almost universally recall Jeffries as a cerebral and studious legislator willing to work with peers of all ideological persuasions. They remember his speeches in conference meetings and the Assembly chamber that, while demonstrating a deep grasp of logic and policy, were delivered only infrequently, as if to maximize their impact.

“He thinks things out like a chess player, four or five moves in advance,” said David Paterson, a Democrat who served as New York governor during some of Jeffries’ tenure in Albany. “To me, he’s like a modern-day Columbo. While you’re putting him down, he’s planning how to take you out.”

As Jeffries now seeks one of the most difficult jobs in American politics, his origin story underscores a broader change in Democratic politics.

Once an insurgent candidate who so thoroughly irked the New York establishment they drew his apartment out of the Assembly district he eventually won, Jeffries is now facing criticism from the party’s left. From their perch, the Democratic leader is out of touch with the issues animating the party base and far too reliant on a bygone way of doing business.

Whether he can prove them wrong will not only write the next chapter of his story. It will influence where the cartoon dust cloud of infighting that is today’s Democratic Party drifts next.

“He comes off as someone who fits more directly into the prior generation: Very buttoned-up, very message-tested talking points,” said one New York Democratic consultant granted anonymity to candidly discuss Jeffries’ political standing. “There’s a handful of issues that are driving the extremes of the party, and he tends to fall squarely into the older thinking on them: Israel is one. Medicare for All is another. I’m not saying the vanguard is right. But he’s not on the vanguard.”

At least, not anymore.

After stints at a white-shoe law firm and as a corporate lawyer for Viacom and CBS, Jeffries launched his first political campaign in 2000 at the age of 29, going hard at incumbent Roger Green over accusations he was failing an Assembly district that included the Brooklyn enclave where Jeffries was born, raised and had moved back to with his wife.

“You’re out of touch,” a mustachioed Jeffries said during a heated debate in which Green later stormed off the set.

Jeffries, a devout Baptist, had brought up Green’s Muslim faith on air, which the incumbent found divisive. It ultimately didn’t matter. Jeffries lost by 18 points.

When New York redrew its Legislative boundaries two years later, Jeffries was meticulously notched out of the seat, an act of institutional retribution for his perceived insolence, giving him an early taste for creative line-drawing that has parallels to today’s redistricting wars between Democrats and Republicans. He challenged the incumbent anyway, this time with even worse results.  

It wasn’t until Green gave up his seat to run for Congress that Jeffries won in 2006 after moving back into the redrawn 57th District.

Scott Levenson, head of political consulting and lobbying firm the Advance Group, was hired by Jeffries on those early campaigns and said his client had a congenital predisposition for public service: His mother was a social worker and his father was a state substance abuse counselor. Politics, activism, Black history and the expectation of academic achievement were very much discussed at the dinner table.

“He comes from an active political family,” Levenson said in an interview. “He didn’t grow up in the restaurant business.”

Even back then, Levenson said, Jeffries was exhibiting qualities that would come to define him in Congress.

“The guy bangs the phone all the time; and he’s got a nice way about him, so people want to talk to him,” Levenson said of Jeffries’ efforts to raise money and build coalitions. “I talk to Republicans who don’t hear bombastic, they hear thoughtful and balanced. And with the margin he’s going to be served, that’s probably a good thing.”

In January 2007, at long last, Jeffries arrived in Albany as a backbench legislator. What he found was the country’s third-largest public institution — second only to the federal government and the State of California — in chaos.

The state Capitol during that era was riven by Democratic infighting and scandal — giving Jeffries a front row seat for how dysfunction and small majorities can dash legislative dreams and how more disciplined institutions can fill the power vacuum.

Beginning in 2009, Democrats spent an unhappy two years leading the state Senate, an era marred by intraparty feuds and a debilitating leadership coup. Several senators would go on to be accused of engaging in public corruption during these years.

The governor, Eliot Spitzer, charged into office as a national political celebrity, only to squander that momentum by waging war with Democrats and Republicans alike. He resigned in 2008 in the middle of a prostitution scandal, paving the way for Paterson, his lieutenant, to take over for the remainder of his term.

The brunt of governing fell to Jeffries’ colleagues in the Democratic-dominated state Assembly.

“It definitely weighed on the Assembly that we were the adult institution in the room,” said Rory Lancman, a colleague who worked with Jeffries on several pieces of legislation. “But also, that meant we could dictate terms to an unusual degree.”

By that time, the chamber had been led for over a decade by the powerful Manhattan Democrat Sheldon Silver. His top-down approach — deciding which bills came to the floor for a vote, doling out leadership stipends to allies and punishing dissenters — rankled lawmakers. But Silver, who would be ousted from power in 2015 after being accused of felony fraud and corruption, maintained one of the few stable centers of power in Albany until Andrew Cuomo’s election as governor in 2010.

It was in this atmosphere — a combination of deep Democratic Party disarray and iron-fisted rule — that Jeffries came of political age before ever working under the velvet-gloved iron fist of California Rep. Nancy Pelosi and prosecuting Trump’s first impeachment.

By the numbers, Jeffries was a middle-of-the-pack legislator, according to a POLITICO analysis of his performance in 2011, his penultimate year in office. He sponsored 87 bills (the 27th most in a 99-person Democratic conference), backed four that were approved by both houses of the Legislature (45th) and voted the same way as leadership 98 percent of the time (62nd).

In his final year in the statehouse, Jeffries was fighting an intense congressional primary against then-New York City Council member Charles Barron. As is common for state lawmakers seeking higher office, he missed 75% of votes in the Assembly.

But numbers aren’t everything in the state Capitol, where much of the action takes place behind closed doors. Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, Silver’s successor, said Jeffries’ oratory supporting legislation to change the way prison inmates are counted in the U.S. Census stood out. That measure, which tallied people according to their home communities rather than the districts where they were imprisoned, ultimately passed as part of Paterson’s state budget.

“There’s certain legislators where, when there’s a debate that they’re in, you stop whatever you’re doing because they have such command of the issues,” Heastie said.

Jeffries, he added, “is one of the best communicators I’ve seen in my 26 years in the Legislature.”

While in Albany, Jeffries also began to develop an understanding of legislative institutions, which would go on to aid his meteoric rise in Congress.

Several years into his tenure in the state Capitol, Democratic Rep. Yvette Clarke called a meeting of Black elected officials in Brooklyn to address one of the most explosive issues of the day: The NYPD’s use of stop-and-frisk to target mostly Black and Latino men for invasive and often public searches.

At the time, police officers were on track to stop and frisk more than a half-million New Yorkers with nearly no criminal charges to show for it. Clarke wanted something done.

At the close of the meeting, members of the New York Civil Liberties Union approached Jeffries with an idea, according to Donna Lieberman, executive director of the organization since 2001: Would the assemblymember carry legislation to bar the NYPD from electronically retaining identifying information about people stopped and released without further legal action?

Jeffries agreed, and, after introducing the bill, gave what several colleagues recalled as a stirring floor speech about the need for urgent action. The initiative turned out to be a relatively easy sell in the deep-blue Assembly. It was in the state Senate, where Democrats had just won a narrow and ultimately fleeting majority, where one of Jeffries’ most memorable legislative victories was at risk.

Selecting a cosponsor in the other chamber is an art unto itself. A successful pick requires knowing alliances, rivalries and the proclivities of leadership in a separate legislative body. Jeffries’ decision demonstrated all of those things, according to one person involved in negotiations who was granted anonymity to discuss private deliberations. But it also showed a willingness to reach outside his circle of core allies — in this case, by tapping Eric Adams, then a freewheeling state senator with an overlapping district and, years later, New York City’s mayor.

The two men have long had a cool relationship, even if they’ve mostly praised each other in public. Polar opposites in style, they had backed different candidates for city comptroller and public advocate in 2009 and would go on to fight numerous other proxy battles over the years.

In 2010, though, Adams, a former police captain, stood in well as a credible messenger and outspoken critic of overpolicing. During closed-door Senate Democratic conference meetings, according to the person involved in the bill negotiations who spoke with POLITICO, Adams would patiently explain to members vulnerable to pressure from police unions why stop-and-frisk was not actually improving public safety.

Jeffries, meanwhile, agreed to limit the bill’s scope to New York City to garner support from upstate members.

“I think he was very shrewd,” said the person involved in the bill negotiations. “He was feeling his way into the politics of it and trying to get a read of how things were cutting.”

The bill’s passage gave both Jeffries and Adams a major legislative win, propelling their careers on upward trajectories and sparking a last-ditch and ultimately unsuccessful push for a gubernatorial veto from Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his police commissioner, Raymond Kelly.

“Stop-and-frisk was becoming a national issue, and the NYPD, love ’em or hate ’em, is a force to be reckoned with,” Lieberman said, recalling Jeffries’ work on the legislation. “This was his first foray onto the national stage. It was important for him.”

Manhattan Democratic Chair Keith Wright, a former state assemblymember, summed up Jeffries’ Albany years by recalling longstanding bipartisan basketball games in which they both participated.

“He didn’t have to be the one scoring the points, but he was down underneath the basket getting the rebound,” Wright said, noting that Jeffries was not a trash-talker. “He was making sure other people were scoring the points.”

That approach has proven fruitful. During his latter years in state government, he was already drawing comparisons to Barack Obama. And once he got to Congress, he rocketed up the pecking order to become chair of the House Democratic Caucus in just six years before being elected minority leader at the end of 2022.

It may not have been fast enough to keep up with an increasingly fractured Democratic Party.

While he enjoys strong support among House Democrats broadly, the Jeffries school of politics is already seen as passé by the young activist class, portending a potentially difficult speakership that will require him to manage factions with deeply disparate goals. The left sees him as too deferential to Israel supporters and has criticized him for taking his name off Medicare for All legislation after co-sponsoring it for years.

Ironically, though, it's a dynamic Jeffries has dealt with his entire career, according to Basil Smikle Jr., the former head of the New York State Democratic Party and generational peer of the presumptive House speaker.

Green, the Assembly incumbent Jeffries ran such a spirited campaign against, got his start in the civil rights movement. And along with an entire generation of Black activists, he paved the way for younger leaders like Jeffries. That generational transfer of power, however, did not always come easily, according to Smikle.

Ambitious young New Yorkers like Jeffries, who broke with the establishment to endorse Obama for president in 2008, were eager to have their shot at shaping government. Battle-hardened activists, though, remained skeptical of their juniors, who came of age long after the struggles against racism, voter suppression, segregation and outright violence began.

“In a way, it has come full circle,” Smikle said. “Hakeem has had to prove himself as an activist throughout history. And he’s still trying to prove that he has that muscle.”

Madison Fernandez contributed to this report.

item.title: No clear challengers for Chuck Schumer’s post, barring a midterm catastrophe
item.description: If there’s a Democratic majority in the Senate, the New Yorker will almost certainly lead it. If not, buckle up.

media:content.media:title: "I think people recognize that we have had a lot of success," Schumer recently said about Democrats' improving midterm odds.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Calen Razor
item.content:encoded:
Chuck Schumer is about to find out what his path to keeping power looks like.

If Democrats win a Senate majority in Tuesday's midterms, pulling off what was once seen as a longshot feat, senators and aides across the caucus agree the New Yorker is a shoo-in to return as top leader — rebuffing critics who have lambasted how he has handled President Donald Trump.

“Schumer delivering a Democratic Senate certainly justifies another term as leader,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), capturing the consensus sentiment.

But if Democrats fail to meet their recently expanded expectations, Schumer could be in for a bumpier path back to power.

If Democrats manage to end up with fewer seats — a scenario most in the party consider highly unlikely as polling continues to move away from Republicans — outside progressive groups that have been gearing up to demand a leadership change regardless of the election outcome could suddenly find traction among the senators who will decide Schumer’s fate.

Multiple factions believe Schumer will hold on as leader, however, so long as his party picks up seats — though it might not be without some internal horsetrading and headaches.

“This isn’t last year,” said a Schumer-neutral Senate Democratic aide granted anonymity to speak about internal caucus dynamics, referring back to government funding fights with Trump that had many Democratic senators publicly fuming over how Schumer handled them.

But if Democrats are in the minority, the 75-year-old leader could find himself dealing with members who publicly break with him, questions from colleagues about whether he will retire in 2028 or even an unlikely longshot challenger, according to five people interviewed about Schumer’s standing.

Senate Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December, and Schumer declined to discuss in a recent interview how he plans to campaign for another two years as top dog, saying he was focused solely on the midterms.

“Look, I have focused totally like the North Star on winning back the Senate. And I think people recognize that we have had a lot of success,” Schumer told reporters in late September when asked about his critics.

The challenge for Schumer is the election map remains volatile in the final stretch before Election Day.

Democrats are confident they’ll pick up one seat from Republicans — in North Carolina, where Schumer personally recruited former Gov. Roy Cooper to run. They’re cautiously optimistic about a host of other Republican-held states, including Ohio, Iowa and Texas — where the establishment’s preferred nominees all won.

However, some races where Democrats have had high hopes continue to hang in the balance — including Maine, where the party's initial nominee, Graham Platner, imploded, with replacement Troy Jackson struggling to gain distance from GOP incumbent Susan Collins. The Michigan race remains in margin-of-error territory with Democrats locked in eleventh-hour infighting. Rep. Haley Stevens, the Schumer-backed candidate who lost the Democratic primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday over hard-left Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

Meanwhile, the Alaska race has been rocked in recent days by a New York Times report that national Democratic operatives schemed to recruit a same-named candidate to confuse voters who would otherwise support Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Schumer said last week he had no knowledge of or participation in the effort.

Many of the factors that will decide the election lie well outside of Schumer’s control, and while Schumer's standing has improved as Republicans’ fortunes have dimmed, he is still the subject of latent dissatisfaction in corners of the party’s ranks.

Schumer could also be welcoming freshmen who have been critical of his leadership.

Illinois Democrat Juliana Stratton, who is poised to win her Senate race next week, will not support Schumer for leader, according to her spokesperson. Neither would Minnesota Senate hopeful Peggy Flanagan, whose spokesperson reiterated her position that “we need a progressive champion to lead Senate Democrats and that's not Chuck Schumer.”

Schumer will likely make the case he helped Democrats win seats regardless of the outcome by pointing to his recruiting coups and the hundreds of millions of dollars in financial support he’s directed to candidates — including those like Jackson and El-Sayed who weren’t his first picks. Spokespeople for the two men did not respond to a request for comment on whether they would support Schumer for leader.

Some Democrats speculate that blame for a narrow failure to retake the majority could fall not on Schumer but on the Senate Democratic campaign arm and its current chair, his fellow New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand.

Schumer can also count on a deep well of support among his colleagues, built on more than two decades of involvement in recruiting, fundraising and otherwise overseeing the Senate Democratic political apparatus.

“He's done a good job in terms of helping to recruit great candidates for us to get the majority,” Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) said of Schumer, while adding Democrats need to “get the majority” before talking about internal leadership.

Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) also told POLITICO that she is supporting Schumer, and another Democratic senator, granted anonymity given the sensitivity of the leadership discussions, added there was “every indication” Schumer will be again elected leader.

A major complication for Schumer’s critics is that no one else appears eager to take on what is frequently a thankless job, despite months of calls from outside groups and some House Democrats for an alternative candidate. The leadership election will be conducted by secret ballot, giving lawmakers the shield of anonymity — and Schumer needs only a simple majority of Democratic senators to win.

There’s also a concern that a leadership fight would distract from Trump, the Iran conflict and looming end-of-year legislative battles, with some suggesting critics could instead lobby for caucus changes or other commitments that would let them say they secured concessions from Schumer.

“Is there someone running against Schumer that I don’t know about?” said Sen. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico when asked if he’d back Schumer for leader. “You can’t defeat someone if there’s not a challenger. Before there’s a race, there has to be at least two folks running for it.”

Some progressive groups see Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, previously the No. 3 Senate Democrat, as a possible bridge away from Schumer, but she is not planning to run, according to a person granted anonymity to speak about her plans. Nor is Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who is running for the No. 2 slot.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is currently the No. 5 Senate Democrat, is now eyeing a move up but not the top job. A spokesperson for Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, who is currently No. 4, declined to comment.

But Booker said during a CNN appearance last week that “you’ve got to give” praise to Schumer for the midterms, calling him a “key player in making sure we have a real strategy to win back the United States Senate.”

Lower down the ladder, Sen. Adam Schiff is interested in a leadership bid, according to a person close to the Californian who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Democrats also view Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey as another potential future member of the leadership team.

Even the handful of members who have been most vocal about wanting to help direct the party’s future — some of them eyeing presidential bids in 2028 — are so far keeping their powder dry.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), for instance, responded to speculation he might mount a run for leader by saying “that has just not been my focus.”

“My focus has been on what the Democratic Party will stand for in 2028 and winning back the White House in 2028,” he said in an interview. Pressed on whether he’ll support Schumer, he added, “At this point I just want to see … the outcome of the 2026 midterms.”

item.title: Facing a Trump backlash, New York Republicans blame blue state incumbents
item.description: GOP candidates are facing a tough political environment this year with an unpopular president in the White House.

media:content.media:title: New York Republicans are arguing that Albany, not President Donald Trump, is the root of voters' woes.

item.dc:creator: By Nick Reisman
item.content:encoded:
ALBANY, New York — New York Republicans have a closing argument for voters unhappy with the cost of living: Blame the incumbent Democrats who run Albany.

President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity in his native state — made worse by high gas prices and a Canadian tariff war — has created a nightmare environment for the GOP in this deep blue state. Yet Republican candidates, strategists and former officeholders believe their party can leverage New Yorkers’ vexation with high taxes, housing costs and skyrocketing utility bills to offset the midterm agony their party is poised to suffer on Tuesday.

Gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman’s final TV ad warns voters that Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul’s reelection will result in a tax hike at the behest of her political ally, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. On the trail, he blasts the sharp increase in energy costs and pledges to reverse the state’s 12-year-old ban on natural gas drilling along the Pennsylvania border. And he’s pledging to bolster public safety by repealing a package of criminal justice law changes.

Republicans hope those attacks will offset Democrats’ efforts to make the election a referendum on Trump. GOP candidates running in down-ballot House and state legislative contests have used Hochul as a foil — a reflection of her middling poll numbers for much of the year.

Rep. Mike Lawler, running in a district Trump lost by one point two years ago, has gleefully tied Democrats to Hochul.

“If Democrats in New York complain about affordability, we have the highest state taxes in the country, income and property taxes. We have chronically poor educational performance. We have a housing market that’s stultified,” said former Rep. John Faso, a Republican who ran for governor in 2006. “Since the Democrats have been running New York state at the statewide level for many years — it’s hard to blame all of that on Donald Trump.”

Hochul’s campaign insists New York voters will positively affirm her five years in office.


“From the beginning, this race has been about records: Governor Hochul has put money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, invested $4 billion in public safety, and fought back against Trump’s attacks – all Bruce Blakeman has done is raise taxes, stick his neck out for ICE, and defend everything Trump does,” Hochul campaign spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki said in a statement. "New Yorkers don’t want that and they never have.”


The rhetoric reflects a broader bet about voters’ collective mood in an intensely disruptive political era and is a test of whether increasingly nationalized elections can still hinge on local concerns. Skyrocketing gas and grocery costs, along with the perception among younger people that their generation will not be as financially secure as their parents, has fueled insurgent primary candidates’ successful bids against their establishment foes.

New York Republicans are making this anti-incumbent case eight years after Democrats won the state Senate, giving them control of both legislative chambers and the governor’s office. GOP officials contend that Democratic control in Albany has made the Empire State less safe and more expensive. They hope the argument will appeal to swing voters, including the growing number of people who aren’t enrolled in a party, and disaffected Democrats concerned with the party’s leftward lurch — especially after Mamdani’s election.

The stakes for Republicans extend beyond Blakeman’s longshot bid for governor. The GOP is trying to retain control of the closely divided House, and New York is home to several swing districts.

Republicans are fretting about the political fate of Lawler, who occupies one of those swing seats. They are also nervously watching the outcome of a race for a deep red House seat being vacated by Rep. Elise Stefanik — an election that was never expected to be competitive.

Polls have shown their entire statewide ticket, which is led by Blakeman and includes state attorney general and comptroller candidates, down by double digits against the incumbent Democrats. One survey also showed the limits of both candidates’ affordability pitches: 35% of likely voters said neither would make life more affordable for average New Yorkers, compared with 30% who chose Hochul and 27% who chose Blakeman.

Voters across the country are enraged by the cost of living, and Hochul’s allies expect they will take it out on Trump.

“When you have a level of anger at the government or life, sometimes that spills out on people who aren’t to blame,” said Democratic former New York City Council Speaker Christine Quinn. “But in New York as it relates to Gov. Hochul, that misplaced anger is easily dispelled when voters are reminded of everything she’s gotten done.”

Some Republicans acknowledge that voters may be in a sour enough mood to reject GOP incumbents like Lawler along with Democrats. That’s added another layer of uncertainty for a party that’s desperate to regain statewide relevance.

“This is the craziest and weirdest election cycle that I've ever seen,” said Chris Tague, a state lawmaker and local GOP party chair. “It’s been very tough to gauge what’s going to happen on Tuesday night.”

Republicans are nevertheless trying to find ways of returning to power by casting this midterm fight as a change election.

GOP state attorney general candidate Saritha Komatireddy, running against two-term Democrat Letitia James, has framed her race entirely around public safety as her campaign makes an overt appeal to voters across the political spectrum concerned with crime.

“New Yorkers are tired of the way things are going,” Komatireddy said. “They understand things are going in the wrong direction. They want change.”

The state’s notoriety for high taxes has also given Republicans ammunition.

Blakeman has warned that Hochul’s second term will include the tax hikes being sought by Mamdani, her democratic socialist ally in City Hall. The mayor and his political base — which Hochul needs to run up the score in the five boroughs — are expected to pressure the governor next year to raise income tax rates on rich people and large corporations. Hochul has insisted Mamdani’s campaigning for her is not linked to a promise to back an increase.

In one of his final TV spots, Blakeman’s campaign contends Hochul is to blame for voters’ affordability woes.

“Kathy Hochul made New York unaffordable — taxing paychecks, toll and fare hikes. The nation’s highest taxes,” the ad’s narrator says.

While Hochul has not definitively ruled out a tax increase next year, the Republican nominee has proposed eliminating taxes for most New Yorkers — though he has not spelled out the details.

A party that in the 1990s simultaneously held the governor’s mansion, New York City Hall and a U.S. Senate seat has witnessed its power rapidly erode this century. A New York Republican last won a statewide race in 2002, when George Pataki secured a third term. Trump’s first midterm in 2018 saw the final toehold of GOP power erased when the party lost the state Senate.

Republicans have seen their statewide enrollment steadily dwindle as well, with more voters now registered as independents. Redoubts of Republican power are confined to some upstate counties and on bellwether Long Island, where Blakeman is a top official.

Four years ago, then-Rep. Lee Zeldin made it within 6 points of unseating Hochul — the closest a Republican has come in a gubernatorial election since the GOP’s losing streak began in 2006.

Even that race highlighted the difficulty of a GOP victory in New York. Hochul had taken office only a year earlier and was not as well known as her predecessor, Andrew Cuomo. Democratic President Joe Biden’s popularity was starting to wane. And Republicans benefitted from the deep pockets of cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder, who funded a super PAC to boost their nominee.

Zeldin still lost. And Hochul has used the race as an example of how her party can’t take anything for granted.

“We have major pockets of truly MAGA Republicans,” she told podcaster Ben Max recently. “It’s a much more purple state than people would think."

Still, Democrats have enjoyed the trappings of incumbency that make it difficult for Republicans to break through as New York’s political establishment remains behind Hochul.

The governor, a powerhouse fundraiser, has handily outspent Blakeman on advertising by more than $10 million, according to data from the ad tracking firm AdImpact. New York’s deep-pocketed private sector — including business leaders who need a powerful governor on their side in Albany — have largely stuck with Hochul. Labor organizations that once endorsed incumbent Republicans like Pataki are firmly within her camp.

“They play a role in this,” said New York Conservative Party Chair Gerard Kassar. “They definitely play a role in keeping incumbents in.”

item.title: Chris Murphy is hospitalized after stroke
item.description: “He is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” the Connecticut Democrat's top aide said.

media:content.media:title: Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) ascends on an escalator on his way to a vote at the U.S. Capitol on July 30, 2026.

item.dc:creator: By Meredith Lee Hill and Jordain Carney
item.dc:contributor: By Meredith Lee Hill and Jordain Carney
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Murphy is being hospitalized following a stroke, an aide to the Connecticut Democrat said Sunday.

“Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” Allison Herwitt, Murphy’s chief of staff, said in a statement.

“He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” she added.

Murphy, who is viewed as a potential 2028 White House candidate, has been traveling the country to campaign for candidates, including recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He had been previously scheduled to attend campaign events in New Hampshire on Sunday.

His staff began notifying people Saturday afternoon of the hospitalization and stroke, a person told POLITICO at the time.

Murphy is the latest lawmaker to face public health issues while in office. Former Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) was hospitalized earlier this year and absent from the Capitol for months. Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-N.J.) also had an unexplained monthslong absence that he later said was due to depression.

Murphy is one of several sitting senators who have experienced strokes in recent years.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said in 2022 that he had been hospitalized by a minor stroke. Sen. Ben Ray Lujan (D-N.M.) was also hospitalized that same year for a stroke. Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), then a Senate candidate, also had a stroke in 2022 that he later described as near fatal. Then-Sen. Mark Kirk, a Republican of Illinois, suffered a stroke in 2012.

Fetterman said in an X post Sunday he was "rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery."

"As someone who survived a near-fatal stroke, I understand all too well how much this impacts your life," he said.

Murphy joined the Senate in 2013 and quickly became a leading advocate within the chamber on stricter gun regulation laws after the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting occurred just weeks after he won his 2012 Senate race. Murphy held the Senate floor for nearly 15 hours in 2016 to demand stricter gun laws.

Murphy’s also been a prominent figure within the Senate Democratic caucus on foreign policy. More recently, he’s urged his party to be more aggressive in its strategies for checking President Donald Trump. Murphy warned at a Middle East Institute event last week that Trump could try to restart the Iran war after the election. He’s also a junior member of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s leadership team.

Before joining the Senate, Murphy spent six years in the House.

item.title: GOP starts coming to terms with a lame-duck Donald Trump
item.description: A Election Day “shellacking,” one GOP lawmaker said, will have the president “looking for our help more than we’d be looking for his.”

media:content.media:title: Trump, seen among Senate leaders during a June visit to the Capitol, could see quick tests of his post-election influence.

item.dc:creator: By Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.dc:contributor: By Jordain Carney and Mia McCarthy
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump will have his ironclad grip on congressional Republicans tested like never before if the party loses one or both chambers Tuesday.

Trump already appears to be gearing up to blame others if Democrats retake the House or the Senate. But within the halls of the Capitol, GOP lawmakers are contemplating whether the president’s ability to bend them to his whims will diminish if the party is swept out of power.

“We’ll see,” Rep. Lloyd Smucker (R-Pa.) said when asked how much influence the president will have after the midterms, before praising Trump’s record and willingness to hit the campaign trail on behalf of Republican candidates.

Granted anonymity to speak frankly before the election, many of the 15 GOP lawmakers interviewed about the future of Trump’s influence said they believe his days of dictating outcomes with Truth Social posts and late-night phone calls could be coming to an end.

“It's not like his persuasion is growing,” said a Republican senator. “Political capital is earned and lost the same way.”

One House Republican cast the potential fight for minority leader as an early test of Trump’s sway: “One would say that the president would have quite a bit of influence on who leads in the minority. But one would also say that he has less influence because some people would blame him” for a loss.

The member added: “That will be an interesting dynamic after Election Day. No one expects Trump to take any blame after the election. So if he doesn't, who does?”

It’s hardly the first time Republicans have predicted that Trump’s days of dominating the GOP were on the wane. A broad swath of the party turned on him after the Capitol attack on Jan. 6, 2021, only to come back to the fold as he regained power.

Despite plenty of kvetching publicly and privately about some of Trump's policies and personnel picks since being sworn in for a second term, most in the party have fallen in line — and few expect him to change his high-pressure style during his final two years in office.

Many Republicans anticipate he'll weigh in on 2028 congressional primaries while also playing a loud role in determining the party’s presidential nominee — as well as weighing in on day-to-day machinations on Capitol Hill.

“He’s going to continue fully engaged … regardless of the outcome,” Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso said in an interview, praising Trump’s “very creative” and “thoughtful” ideas on domestic and foreign affairs.

Rep. Chris Smith (R-N.J.) said in an interview “it'll be challenging” for Trump if Republicans lose the House but said his influence would persist: “He still has the bully pulpit, and I say that in a good way.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump “is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

But unlike Trump’s last midterm drubbing, in 2018, a decisive loss this time would officially usher him into lame-duck status. While House members will all be campaigning for reelection with Trump still in office — and face the prospect of a presidential primary threat — only about a third of currently sitting Republican senators are in the same boat.

The rest will stand for reelection in 2030 and 2032, after Trump is out of office.

One GOP senator pointed to the party’s stable of vulnerable candidates and incumbents who have broken with Trump over the Iran conflict as a sign of things to come if Republicans take a battering Tuesday.

“He’s in trouble,” the senator said.

Another House Republican added that if Democrats win only a small majority in that chamber, Trump will “still carry a lot of sway.” But a “shellacking,” the lawmaker said, will have Trump “looking for our help more than we’d be looking for his.”

“If it’s truly a big blue wave, every committee will investigate the hell out of him the next two years and R’s will quickly start looking at [2028] and beyond,” the member added in a text message.

Trump will face a series of quick tests after the midterms. The House is expected to vote on whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth soon after members return. Some Republicans said if voters deliver a wipeout for their party amid widespread dissatisfaction with the Iran war, several of their colleagues could end up supporting the measure.

The president could also face headwinds if he tries to muscle a final party-line spending bill through Congress before Democrats take charge in either chamber and kill any chance for partisan legislation like the election bill known as the SAVE America Act. Republicans have already struggled to move these measures, and GOP lawmakers who just lost reelection could have little reason to rally behind them on their way out the door.

House Republicans are in particular keeping their eyes on whether Trump will weigh in on the GOP leadership races that will play out in the week after the election.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan of Ohio are expected to clash if Republicans are electing a minority leader. But many GOP lawmakers think Speaker Mike Johnson could have a shot at hanging on as the chamber's top Republican if Trump wants it.

Jordan and Scalise are also both close Trump allies, and most Republicans are skeptical he would choose between the two.

“The president of the United States certainly has influence,” Jordan said in an interview. “I think he'll continue to have influence.”

In the Senate, conservatives are privately questioning whether Trump will blame Senate Majority Leader John Thune if Republicans lose control of the chamber.

Trump sowed doubt about Thune’s leadership over the summer as he stewed about the Senate’s failure to act on the elections bill. But he more recently publicly defended Thune during the party’s midterm convention in September.

Many Republican senators expect Thune to keep his job even if Trump moves against him. Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) has aired frustrations about how the Senate is run but has repeatedly said he won’t run for leader and has declined to criticize Thune. Some GOP senators have privately speculated about whether Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) has leadership ambitions, but few think he’s actually interested.

Trump turning on Thune “certainly would not” cause Thune to lose his leadership race, said one of the GOP senators, adding that it was “absolutely the case” that Thune would keep his job even if Trump balks.

Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who is in line to run the Senate GOP campaign arm in the next Congress, said of Thune, “I don't think there's an insurgent movement that's against him.”

Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican, is backing Thune as well. Asked about the speculation that Trump could turn on Thune, Barrasso said, “He’s going to get reelected as leader.”

item.title: ‘Look what I brought home for you’: GOP embraces earmark revival as Election Day looms
item.description: Republican lawmakers in the country’s tightest races are bragging about “bringing home the bacon” to a sour electorate.

media:content.media:title: Rep. Bill Huizenga departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol on April 29, 2025.

item.dc:creator: By Jennifer Scholtes
item.content:encoded:
With voters sour on Republican governance, GOP candidates in the most competitive House and Senate races are reaching for a time-tested message that has grown out of fashion in their party: bringing home the federal bacon.

A POLITICO analysis of the dozen closest congressional races for Republican incumbents revealed that most are highlighting earmark success stories in the final days before voters head to the polls.

The ability to secure federal funding for pet projects back home — something many in the GOP have spent years trying to curtail — has given those candidates a positive talking point as President Donald Trump’s flagging approval ratings and widespread voter dissatisfaction over issues like the Iran war, high gas prices and tariffs weigh on other messages.

“When the president's job approval is in the 30s, it is helpful for Republican candidates to be able to create some distance from the president. It's challenging to do that without encouraging the president's wrath,” Republican pollster Whit Ayres said in an interview. “But focusing on bringing home the bacon might be one very good way to do it without antagonizing the president.”

In Michigan, Rep. Tom Barrett is out with an ad about a $750,000 earmark for youth mentoring; in New York, Rep. Mike Lawler is talking about how he secured $120 million for local projects.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania is telling voters he has “brought back more than $110 million to our community,” including millions in earmarks, while Rep. David Valadao has run ads showcasing $500 million in earmarks for water projects in California’s Central Valley.

Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a GOP moderate seeking to project independence from Trump in a competitive contest, has repeatedly touted the exact count of the earmarks she has locked in over the last half-decade for her home state of Maine.

The sum: 672 projects totaling $1.5 billion, “from Madawaska to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford,” as she said in her opening statement earlier this month in her first debate against Democrat Troy Jackson. This past week, Collins has peppered voters with county-specific text messages detailing how much she’s secured for each area.

There are countless other examples of earmark campaigning among vulnerable Republican incumbents, though many conservatives remain reluctant to associate themselves with the practice. It still carries a stigma of corruption after two Republicans were sent to prison on related bribery charges in the mid-2000s, paving the way for the GOP to do away with earmarks in 2011.

That left GOP candidates unable to play up the clearest spoils of incumbency ahead of the “blue wave” of 2018. But Democrats revived them in 2021 with new safeguards, and now Republicans are taking advantage as they navigate another tough midterm cycle.

“That word ‘earmark’ can carry some negative baggage, especially among the old fiscal conservatives,” nonpartisan pollster Mike Noble said in an interview. “But when you describe that same expenditure as funding for a local water system, highway, public safety project — voters evaluate that differently.”

Recognizing the advantages, Republicans opted to keep earmarks around under unified party leadership in 2025, resulting in the enactment of almost $16 billion worth of earmarks this year. For those who still consider earmarks anathema to the GOP’s values of fiscal restraint, it’s causing complications on the trail.

Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan is fielding criticism for not requesting any earmarks for his district. While he airs ads calling himself “tight with a buck,” his opponents are telling voters that lawmakers like Huizenga are increasing their net worth “while turning down community project funding.”

Some recent polling shows Huizenga trailing his Democratic challenger, state Sen. Sean McCann, by 1 percentage point.

McCann said in an interview he will “go to bat” for earmarks if he defeats Huizenga: “That's an expectation that people have when you want to represent them — that you do the things that are important and secure crucial investments for the district.”

Huizenga defended himself in a statement, saying “earmarks have a long history of waste and abuse by politicians looking to enrich themselves in office.”

Huizenga noted that he has “helped secure hundreds of millions in federal investments for Southwest Michigan without requesting a single earmark,” including a $400 million grant last year for a nuclear power plant and $51 million for a housing redevelopment project.

He isn’t the only Republican incumbent in a tight race who has foregone earmarks. Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is facing a competitive challenge from former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, refused to request cash for district-specific projects as part of the annual government funding process. Instead, he points to his support for efforts made possible through the 2021 infrastructure law signed by then-President Joe Biden, as well as other legislation and grants the Trump administration doles out for local efforts.

Trump officials have traveled to Alaska in recent weeks to stand alongside Sullivan in announcing the delivery of hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding for the state, including $38 million in energy grants and $250 million for rail infrastructure.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who appears to be in a dead heat with his Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, also didn’t ask for any federal funding this year. But he is getting flak for seeking a $4.2 million earmark in 2024 to finance improvements to increase water to a wildlife refuge that borders his ranch.

Spokespeople for the Sullivan and Marshall campaigns did not respond to requests for comment.

Whether voters perceive earmark requests as positive or negative likely depends heavily on how a candidate frames the talking point, Noble said, acknowledging that incumbents rarely use the word in campaign ads or town hall speeches and instead speak broadly about how they “deliver” for their district.

“Voters, at the end of the day — it's about direct benefit. What are they getting out of this deal? That's one of the powers of incumbency. They have that ability to say, ‘Hey, look what I brought home for you,’” he said. “But again, what else are they going to talk about?”

item.title: Senate Democrats’ top super PAC spends in South Carolina for the first time
item.description: Senate Majority PAC is running digital ads in support of Democrat Annie Andrews in her race against GOP Sen. Darline Graham.
